title: Ramadan: the fast of the tongue
hook: whoever doesn't leave false speech, Allah has no need of his hunger (Bukhari)
tomorrow: The charity of the fast's end

segments.voice: Yesterday: Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power. Your line was better than a thousand months. Did you treat one ordinary hour as if it might be the one? Day one hundred twenty-five.

Four in the afternoon on a Ramadan day. A woman driving home hasn't eaten or drunk since before dawn. Someone cuts her off, hard, and then honks, as if it were her fault. Her hands tighten on the wheel. The words are right there, already in her mouth. She's tired, she's hungry, and the other driver is wrong. Her finger is on the window switch. The tradition has a sentence ready for this exact moment. Two words, in Arabic. Today: the fast of the tongue.
screen: `FOUR IN THE AFTERNOON, NO WATER.` → `SOMEONE CUTS HER OFF.` → `THE WORDS ARE RIGHT THERE.`

segments.voice: Back on day eighteen, you heard a hadith from Bukhari about Ramadan. Here it is again, because today it's the whole point: whoever does not give up false speech and acting on it, Allah has no need of their giving up food and drink. In other words, the stomach isn't the only thing that fasts. A fast with a sharp tongue has missed it. There's another report, in the Sunan of Ibn Majah, that's even blunter: many a person who fasts gets nothing from their fast except hunger. Just hunger. The whole day, and nothing to show but an empty stomach. So what do you do at four in the afternoon, when the words are right there? Another hadith in Bukhari answers it. It says fasting is a shield. And if someone fights with you or insults you while you're fasting, say: I am fasting. In Arabic, inni sa'im: two words. Said twice. Not to them, necessarily. Maybe to yourself. It's a reminder of what you're doing today, and that what you're doing today is bigger than winning this moment. The word Ramadan, you'll remember, comes from a root for scorching heat. Some scholars have read that as the heat that burns away wrongdoing. Whether or not that's the origin, some Muslims hear the month that way: meant to burn off more than appetite. Gossip. Lying. Complaining. The cutting remark. And the hope is that a month of holding the tongue leaves a habit behind, the way a month of early mornings does.
screen: `NO NEED OF THEIR HUNGER.` · `NOTHING BUT HUNGER.` · `SAY: I AM FASTING. TWICE.` · `A HEAT THAT BURNS AWAY WRONG.` · then, large: `THE TONGUE FASTS TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: fast from one unkind word. Think of the person you're most likely to snap at today, or the conversation where your tongue tends to run. Picture it now, clearly: the tone, the moment, the words that usually come. Then picture yourself pausing, and saying, inside, I am fasting. Whether or not you're fasting from food, you can fast from that one word. Breathe out slowly. Let the picture end quietly. The bell holds the time.
Ramadan. The month of fasting, from a root for scorching heat; a fast of the tongue as well as the stomach. Today's word.
Your line: fast with the tongue too. When the sharp word comes today, say instead, even just to yourself: I am fasting. Day one hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: During Ramadan, Muslims try to fast from lying, gossip, arguing and harsh words as well as from food and drink, and some answer provocation with the words 'I am fasting'.

original.note: Arabic: the ninth month, from the root r-m-d, scorching heat.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ramadan is a month of not eating.
what it means: the fast is also of the tongue; a fast with false speech is only hunger.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 1903 and 1894 (the shield, 'I am fasting'), Ibn Majah 1690 (nothing but hunger), and the r-m-d etymology.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1903 (whoever does not give up false speech, Allah has no need of his leaving food and drink)
